speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: TABLING OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON SILK AND MAN-MADE FIBRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table copies in English and in French of a further report which I have received from the chairman of the tariff board relating to reference No. 125 on textiles. I am tabling also a transcript of the evidence presented to the board at its public hearings. This report relates to silk and its products and to man-made fibres and their products. As hon. members know, real silk has long since been reduced to a minor role as compared with synthetic fibres.
Two of the most important of the manmade fibres-viscose and acetate-are derivatives of wood pulp. Most of the others are true synthetics, based on petrochemicals or other hydrocarbons. The tariff board report traces the development of these man-made fibres and describes the increasingly important place which they have come to occupy in the textile industry. It finds that the share of the Canadian market filled by these fibres expanded very rapidly and without any serious interruption from the time of their introduction in the early 20's until 1951. It notes, however, that in the last seven or eight years the adoption of new processes and improved finishes in the cotton industry, coupled with a decline in the price of cotton and wool from the levels which prevailed in 1950, have tended to check the gains being made by synthetic fibres. The board also notes that new technological developments have been taking place at such a rapid pace within the synthetics industry that it may be described as one which is "constantly devouring its own young". The new "miracle fibre" of one day is superseded in public esteem and consumer acceptance by the newer one of tomorrow. This continuity of eclipse, born of invention and discovery, may have left some sections of the industry with excess or obsolescent capacity.
In this report the board has brought together a great deal of valuable information regarding the man-made fibre industry in Canada; its size, its location, its importance in the economy and the state of its financial health. The picture which emerges is one
of diversity rather than uniformity. For this reason the board found it difficult to make unqualified generalizations about the industry. In the report, however, it points out that the industry faces much the same problems as were referred to at length in the report on cotton textiles which I tabled in this house on February 11 of this year, and it emphasizes the following features of the situation:
(1)	There is evidence of world-wide overcapacity for the production and processing of man-made fibres; in the board's view, certain units within the Canadian industry are, by any realistic standard, overexpanded.
(2)	The industry serves a highly selective market, which demands a wide variety in type, construction and finish of products. The efforts of Canadian mills to meet this demand result in shorter runs and higher unit costs than are typical in the United States, their main source of competition.
(3)	In general, the Canadian tariff affords a higher level of protection to the synthetic textile industry than is accorded to the producers of corresponding forms of cotton or wool products. However, this protection varies widely from product to product.
(4)	In recent years, at least, important sections of the industry have not been very profitable.
(5)	None the less, the Canadian man-made fibre industry and the branch of the weaving industry based upon man-made fibres hold a larger share of the domestic market than does either the Canadian cotton industry or the Canadian wool industry.
The board after much deliberation has concluded that anything in the nature of a general increase in customs duties on man-made fibres and products thereof could not be justified. What recommendations it is prepared to make relate largely to proposed adjustments within the existing framework of tariff protection. The recommendations represent an attempt to achieve a more equitable distribution of the protection available within the present general level of duties, and to remove certain anomalies which now exist. The recommendations also provide for the introduction of a simpler and more logical arrangement of the tariff items.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the request made yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition I am tabling the exchange of notes which took place earlier this year between Canada and the United States, indicating that a United States proposal to carry out a good-will cruise with 28 United States naval vessels in the great lakes is not inconsistent with the spirit of the Rush-Bagot agreement of 1817 as applied and interpreted by an exchange of notes in 1946.
In requesting that these notes be tabled the Leader of the Opposition suggested that this exchange of notes modified in some way the Rush-Bagot agreement of 1817 concerning naval forces on the great lakes. I should like

to make it quite clear that this is not the case. An agreed application and interpretation of the Rush-Bagot agreement of 1817 formed the subject of an exchange of notes between Canada and the United States in 1946. This exchange is to be found in the Canadian treaty series of 1946, No. 40. As a matter of fact, each year Canada and the United States indicate to each other their respective intentions to carry out naval training exercises in the great lakes.
Perhaps the house would wish that these notes be printed in Hansard. If so there would be no objection to that being done.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw the minister's attention to one or two factors concerning the operation of Canadian National Telegraphs and their management of the northern communications system in the Yukon and British Columbia.
The Department of Transport and Canadian National Telegraphs constitute the second largest federal government employer in the Yukon, and questions relating to the welfare of personnel are very important. Certain unintentional, I am sure, discriminations exist in the northern allowance regulations in various sectors of the operations of Canadian National Telegraphs. I quite realize that Canadian National Telegraphs is a crown corporation and that any regulations concerning northern allowances must be arrived at as a result of discussion and agreement between Canadian National Railways and the telegraphers' union, and that any change in allowances can only be made as the result of negotiations between the management of the company and the union.
However, perhaps it might be suggested to the management of Canadian National that they take the initiative in bringing this matter to a head. C.N.T. employees in the north are required to live under the same conditions as other government employees, yet they are not given the same treatment extended to employees of the Department of Transport. Northern allowances are a factor which could be improved so far as employees of Canadian National Telegraphs in the Yukon are concerned.

Another matter which would bear some investigation is the question of housing for C.N.T. employees, particularly the standard of housing, the rents charged and the facilities offered in relation to the housing supplied to other federal government employees in the area. As I have said, I realize that Canadian National Telegraphs is a crown corporation and a separate entity, but again I urge the minister to consider action to place C.N.T. employees on a plane equal to that of other government employees in the area. This applies not only to housing and northern allowances but to all other benefits. As I view the matter, Mr. Chairman, the only way any effective action can be taken is for the minister to suggest to the management of the C.N.R. that they take the initiative in bringing about these improvements.
The other matter I wish to raise under this item is the question of communications between White Horse and north central and northern Yukon. I am referring now specifically to the implementation of land lines communications between these points.
Several years ago, under the previous administration, the capital of the Yukon was moved from Dawson City down to Whitehorse. The excuse given was that Dawson City lacked the communications necessary to support the capital, and the people there still remember this. Their argument was, why were the communications not brought up to that area? I have been urging for about two years now that the department implement land lines communications to Dawson City and the Mayo area, including Elsa, Calumet and Keno.
Apart from the essential services that communications themselves provide the people in those areas, it is of advantage from this point of view; that C.B.C. radio is possible on an economic basis only if land line facilities are available. Low power repeater transmitters can be installed to give coverage to these areas if land lines are established, but not otherwise. Favourable consideration of this submission in the near future could well result in favourable consideration by the C.B.C. of the application for extension of their radio service to this area.
Now, should the Canadian National decide to go ahead with the construction of land line facilities, I have one further point to make. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that Canadian National Telegraphs should not be undertaking the construction of new facilities in competition with private enterprise. I do not believe there would be any quarrel in so far as the maintenance of existing facilities of the crown corporation are concerned.
Supply-Transport
However, when it comes to new construction I feel that a line should be drawn and the government should not enter into open competition with private enterprise. I refer now to the construction of the pole lines.
Should the minister and the Canadian National management feel that the construction of additional communication facilities is justified, I submit these new pole lines should be constructed by private enterprise under tender. The same remarks apply to the construction of new buildings. For many years the Canadian National has been constructing new buildings and has been contracting all the subtrades on a day labour basis. I feel that this is wrong. I feel that this type of construction should be done by public tender.
This would eliminate the undesirable practice which has existed for so long in the past of the government competing with private contractors. This is doubly important in a frontier area such as the Yukon where small contractors are struggling for existence and trying to build themselves up to a point where they can handle anything that comes along. The growth of small, independent contractors should be fostered and developed by wise government policies. I would suggest that one of these government policies should be the cessation of competition which is now being undertaken by government agencies, such as Canadian National Telegraphs, with private enterprise.
There are three questions I desire to ask, Mr. Chairman, but I do not suggest that the information could be supplied today. I should like to know the landed cost of poles used by Canadian National Telegraphs at Watson lake, at Whitehorse and at mile 1202. It is my belief that local timber and local labour could be used to supply these poles for construction work now being carried on in the Yukon, rather than the utilization of poles from outside sources. When I say "outside" I mean British Columbia or Alberta.
The other specific question, Mr. Chairman, refers to the profits of the northwest communications system during the last fiscal year. I should like to know what those profits were. The construction, if I understand this rightly, is to be done by the applicant, and I do not think either of the departments is concerned with it, save that it must be carried out in accordance with the specifications of the Department of Transport.
I think it is important that we have that procedure clearly established, because I agree with the hon. member for Kootenay West that there is a lack of clarity about the duties of the two ministers. One has to do with the operations of the broadcasting corporation and the other with radio facilities. Perhaps the minister would supplement what I have said; I think that might be helpful.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
No, I think the hon. member for Laurier is quite correct and that what he has stated is, in essence, what I said earlier. One might summarize the functions of the

Supply-Transport
two departments as follows. The Department of National Revenue, through the board of broadcast governors, deals with economic matters, and the Department of Transport deals with technical matters.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
Well, that has been cleared up to some extent, thanks to the hon. member for Laurier, who I think has helped us out considerably.
Now I come to another question which fogs me up and I know it fogs up other members, too. That is the question of piped-in television. There is piped-in television in the cities of Nelson and Trail. Apparently it is possible for local companies to get licences from the Department of Transport, but the department does not exercise any control with respect to the prices charged. When you go to the public utilities commission in Victoria they say, "We exercise no control over this; it is licensed by the Department of Transport". There has been considerable complaint in this respect, and I should like to ask the minister if something could not be done in consultation with the appropriate provincial authorities in order that proper responsibility may be accepted.
It seems to me that the department which issues the licences, should have some control over the tariff and fees charged by the licensee.
I do not want to have the minister getting up too frequently and tiring himself out too soon, so my second question is this. I have received correspondence from people who want to establish what they call reflector stations. We have one or two co-operative groups in my constituency, and I understand they want to put a reflector on top of a mountain and reflect signals from the United States down to their patrons in the valleys below. I understand that permission to do this has been refused, because it is against a regulation, or against the law, or something of that kind.
Would the minister mind explaining to the committee the difference in the regulations in so far as they concern these two types of television and second, would he tell us whether something cannot be done with respect to continuity between licensing and the various charges which are being imposed by the organizers of piped-in television, charges which in some cases are exorbitant. A man pays $150 to have the installation in his house. Then he leaves and a new tenant comes in, and this new tenant is required to pay all the installation charges all over again. Then, third, I should like the minister to tell us what is the distinction between piped-in television and reflected television. I understood some time ago that the department

intended to investigate this system of reflected television and see what was to be done about it, but I am still as foggy as ever.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I tried as best I could to follow what the hon. member was saying. In the first place, we do not have any control over the tariffs which a company operating a piped-in television service can charge. That is a free enterprise operation and it is up to the municipality which will be served to decide whether or not the prices charger are fair and reasonable. If they are not, there is no obligation on anyone to subscribe to the service.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I am glad the minister mentioned that. Does he know of any municipalities which regulate the charges with respect to piped-in television?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: When I said "municipality" I had in mind the people in the municipality Who are receiving the service. If they think the charge is too high they do not have to pay for it.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Like the telephone; there is no regulation. What about the other question concerning this reflected television? Companies and small groups have made application for the right to instal what they call a reflector television station; they put reflectors on top of a mountain and reflect the program into the surrounding valleys. Rather that is what they would like to do, but they are not permitted to do it.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: We issue licences for both piped-in television and reflector television, but we do not issue licences just to bring in United States programs of either type if a Canadian program is available. I think in the areas of which the hon. member is speaking there is a piped-in service from Lethbridge available and, as I understand it, he wants us to license a reflector system which would bring in United States programs. Is that correct?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is
piped-in television in the cities of Nelson and Trail, but there are vast expanses of my constituency where there is no television and where there will not be any television even when the C.B.C. transmitter is installed on the summit near Rossland. These people want the right to have some form of television. They got together and collected a certain amount of capital, and they have asked to be allowed to instal reflector equipment. I do not understand the mechanics of it.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:

I think there is a good chance that it would be approved, though of course that is a matter for the board.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I want to inform the minister that an application has been made by one co-operative in my constituency to the Department of Transport, the appropriate department, and the application has been rejected twice.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: To help me, will the hon. member identify the application and supply us with the company's name?

speechtext: It is the Crescent valley or Slocan valley community co-operative.

speechtext:
I have exactly the same
situation-

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Thank you.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I have a case exactly the same as my hon. friend's; and it has to do with Boston Bar in the Fraser valley. subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my answer to the hon. member is that if an application is received and there is no other Canadian television service available, it would certainly receive, I believe, favourable consideration from the board of broadcast governors. I must remind my hon. friend and the hon. member for Kootenay West that that decision is up to the board of broadcast governors to make, and not my department. But I would suggest that those co-operatives or companies get their applications in right away. If the hon. member for Kootenay West says the application is in we will check on it right away.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
The matter was taken up, I think, two or three years ago. During the
Supply-Transport
lunch hour I will look up the correspondence and let the minister have it so he will understand what I am talking about.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Before the item carries, I think my question is one which properly comes under the Minister of Transport. I would like to know what progress has been made?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I am advised that an application was in but that it has been withdrawn.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: An application for what, precisely?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: For television at Grand Falls.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I have not made my position clear. What I wanted to know was whether the department had approved a site and a channel. I am not interested at this stage in the application, because that would go before the board of broadcast governors.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Yes, we did approve a site in this area.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: And a channel?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I should like the minister to tell us whether the regulations permitting the erection of a reflector television station are under the jurisdiction of his department or under the jurisdiction of the C.B.C.?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is government policy designed to protect existing channels for Canadian broadcasting.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: It seems rather strange that in the city of Vancouver they have the privilege of turning the dial and tuning in a United States station, while 100 miles up the coast we cannot get a reflector licence for a United States station. I do not know whether they are trying to keep that part of the country pure Canadian or what.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I would suggest to the hon. member that if he would speak to my officials about this particular case we will give it consideration.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister whether the Department of Transport

Supply-Transport
has jurisdiction over the allocation of channels, and whether the board of broadcast governors made recommendations in connection with satellite television stations.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: The Department of Transport has jurisdiction over the allocation of channels, but before any licence would be issued the board of broadcast governors would have to pass on the application and then pass it back to us for signature.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: If the application is passed by the board of broadcast governors, is that final?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: No; final authority is vested in the government, which means the Minister of Transport.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Do those licences not have to be approved by the governor in council?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Yes, they do. They come to the Minister of Transport and he signs them; then they go forward to the governor in council for final approval.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I thought, because of the way the minister put it, he rather suggested the governor in council was a rubber stamp. Some of us feel that under the present administration, he is.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: No. I was going to say that in so far as the past government was concerned it might be true, but with respect to this government it is far from being true.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
I certainly support the
previous members and also the contentions they have raised relative to the reception of television programs. I may be able to add a little light to what the hon. member for Kootenay West had to say on this matter. I have had this matter under consideration with the Department of Transport and also with the board of broadcast governors. A firm in our area has already piped in television programs, but with the use of a multiplexor-these are rather technical terms- they have requested permission to add channel 4 at Spokane to improve our reception from a point on the microwave system to Moyie mountain.
They also presented a brief on the matter. It is not their intention to use any more frequencies or bands than they are now using, but it would definitely give us much better reception of United States programs. In view of the fact that a good many of our C.B.C. programs originate in the United States and that we have this complex microwave system going across Canada only a few miles away from our own area, this should be made available to us. The companies concerned are not asking the government to spend terrific sums of money to instal this 
multiplexor, but at the same time I feel we should have some consideration from the department so that we can get better television in our area.
We are situated right in the rocky mountains, and it is practically impossible for us to receive programs from Vancouver or from the east, although we do get fair reception from the Lethbridge station. Our programs are piped in by a private company. We have the support of all the chambers of commerce and the various public organizations in the east and also in the west Koot-enays. I understand that the department have included the east and west Kootenay in a study as to the installation of a station, but at the same time I can see that it is going to be quite some time before this becomes a fact. Also there is the present system which does not include television or radio reception to remote areas. In our large district it is practically impossible to get reception that would be of benefit to all of east Kootenay. I should like to ask the minister whether he would give our request to let us tie in with our present microwave system some consideration.
Incidentally, I have a letter on my desk from the department saying that they do not see eye to eye with me. I may say this is not the first time we have not seen eye to eye, but I am going to look into some other angles of the question. At the present time we are within a very short distance of the microwave system, and in my opinion the policy originally laid down for radio and television is now obsolete and I think we should take a long look at it.
I would request the minister to reconsider his stand on the matter because I can see it will be some time before we get a television booster station. By allowing us to connect with the present microwave system we will be able to have better reception of Spokane and other United States programs which are available to many others parts of British Columbia situated to better advantage than we are in Kootenay East, where we are right in the centre of the Rocky mountains.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: In view of what the hon. member has said I will be very glad to give further consideration to his representations.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS

lor radiotelephone calls. This is the same amount that is required for deep sea vessels which range around the world. If the facts as I have stated them are correct, I would ask the minister to give consideration to having the deposit reduced to $10 or $15.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I am advised that the $50 is to cover the charges that are incurred during the year's operations, and the reason it is the same for big and small vessels is that the charges are the same irrespective of the size of the vessel. The charge is made for the service.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Could the minister indicate what type of charge the $50 covers?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: It is for long distance telephone calls that the people who operate these radiotelephones put through our system.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I am glad to see my facts are correct, because that is the point these people are trying to make. All these long distance calls are billed to the fishermen's home. I think the situation is entirely different where you have deep sea vessels ranging around the world and you want to make sure that the calls are paid for. When the charge is made directly to the fishermen's home 1 do not see how that difficulty could arise, and because of that difference I would suggest that a charge of $10 or $15 would be reasonable.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I am advised that we are quite willing to let a group get together and make a community deposit. It is not our intention to require a deposit for any more than we think will be required to cover the charges made for the use of the service through our system.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
Yesterday I asked a question with regard to whether a person who is not a citizen can have a radiotelephone. The minister's answer is on page 4576 of Hansard, and is not too clear. To bring the matter a little more closely to his attention I will read this extract from Pierre Berton's column in the Toronto Star of March 4, 1959. He says:
Oddly enough, the same day a young Danish immigrant, Mr. Earl Fieh from Stouffville came to see me. He has a business which requires a telephone in his car. But he can't get a telephone in his car because he is not a British subject or a Canadian citizen. He could get one by forming a company but that would cost at least $250 in legal fees.
I called the Department of Transport about this and was told that the law dated back before 1936 and had something to do with security-a word used these days to excuse any kind of foolishness. D.O.T. added, in defence of itself, that nobody had made a presentation urging the law be changed. Is it really necessary for Mr. Fich to send a lobby to Ottawa to get rid of an inane and outdated law?
Supply-Transport
Would the minister comment on that?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: The Radio Act requires that the holder of a licence for a radiotelephone be a British subject, but a landed immigrant can be authorized to operate a radiotelephone.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: But he cannot own one in his own business.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: That is right.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Just take this case, for example. I cannot see why this particular chap could not produce some sort of bona fide to prove that he was a good security risk. Is it because of security that the licence will not be issued?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: It is simply a matter of what the law says. The law requires that the holder of a radiotelephone licence shall be a British subject. It is not a question of our making regulations to make it easier for this particular person.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: Let us look at the anomaly here. A young man or young woman comes to this country and cannot become a citizen for five years. They establish themselves very quickly and they may get into a business where they can use a radiotelephone, but they have to circumnavigate the law. In his answer the minister has pointed out that they can circumnavigate it. It seems to me that the law should be changed. I would ask, as Mr. Berton has asked, whether it is necessary to send a lobby here in order to change the law.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: As a matter of fact the hon. gentleman is a member of parliament like the rest of us, and he can introduce a bill to change the law. So can the minister, and I think it would be a good thing if the minister would do so, because it would have more chance of getting through. This law was passed in 1936 when 1 am sure radiotelephones in motor cars were not contemplated at all. It really applied to broadcasting stations and things of that sort. As the hon. member has said, it is an absolutely silly thing to apply it to radiotelephones in motor cars. I would suggest that the hon. member might appeal to the minister to bring in an amendment to the law during the next session. I do not think I would appeal to him to do it at this session.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: We will be very glad to look into the matter further and see if anything can be done in this regard under the regulations.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:

My officials are making a revision in the technical requirements for model control apparatus, which I feel sure will meet with the approval of the model enthusiasts.

Thank you, Mr. Moore, for your kind letter in reference to Babcock products. Since you used the term "too tough" in reference to the Canadian Department of Transport, I shall go along the same lines. Application for approval for all our new equipment has been made some time ago. We are now sitting tight and waiting for results. It must be remembered-
I should like the minister to listen to this.
-that when we did get approval of our old R/C equipment, the approval arrived approximately one year after we had discontinued these units.
It is from examples like this that the minister can see why I feel that maybe his department is not the best department, by any means. I should like to know why you have this situation across Canada. Someone could say that these people are faddists, but there are hundreds of people with these models who like to use radio controls. Surely we could follow the United States system of licensing, which is so simple and straightforward in comparison to ours. It seems to me this particular branch of the department is asleep at the switch.
I should like to ask, is there any way by which you could improve the licensing of these particular models and allow these enthusiasts to have radio equipment?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext:
I am prompted to rise at this point and draw to the attention of the minister a matter which on the face of it might not appear to be very important, but which is in fact important to a large number of people. It stems from a report which_ appeared in the New York Times concerning the Canadian rules governing small boats passing through the canals of the St. Lawrence seaway. I do not wish to hold up the estimates, but I should like to read two paragraphs of this article which appeared in the New York Times on Friday, June 12, 1959, as follows:
Thousands of owners of small pleasure boats have been dismayed to learn that their craft will not be permitted to travel the length of the St. Lawrence seaway.

As a result, many vacation plans must be changed. Several million dollars already spent for construction of marinas on the seaway may be a dubious Investment.
Willis H. Crosswhite, the traffic services officer of the St. Lawrence seaway development corporation, said yesterday in Massena, N.Y., "Under existing regulations boats under 20 feet over-all or less than two tons dead weight cannot go through the Canadian locks.''
"Therefore, with the Canadians controlling 13 of the 15 locks," he explained, the little boats can't make the whole trip. "In fact," he said, "the boats won't be allowed to travel more than 68 miles on water in the seaway, the distance, including approaches, serviced by the two United States locks."
As the minister knows, the two locks on the United States side-the Eisenhower and the Wiley-Dondero locks-permit the movement of these pleasure craft, and in the area which is affected, particularly the Thousand islands area, the Lachine section and the lake St. Francis section, there are a very large number of pleasure craft whose owners would wish to move them through the locks of the seaway.
I know there must be some reason for the attitude which has been taken here, and I presume that safety of navigation has a lot to do with it; but is it not, going to be a little embarrassing for Canada if the United States permits pleasure craft to go through while Canada does not? I thought I should bring this to the attention of the minister so he may have the opportunity to consult with his officials in order to ascertain if the regulations concerning the Canadian section cannot be changed with a view to having uniform navigation rules for both Canada and the United States.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS
speechtext: I will be glad to discuss that question with the officials of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. The reasons for not allowing these very small craft through the locks are two in number. I should say right away that this regulation only applies to boats less than 20 feet in length, and I think we all realize that these are very small craft. It is considered that it is dangerous for these very small boats to be going through the very large locks of the St. Lawrence seaway. The second reason is that these boats can all be very easily transported by trailer behind a ear. It is considered that they can be moved much more quickly and easily by trailer if their owners want to go, for instance, from New York to Georgian bay. But I will be glad to speak to the officials of the seaway authority about this matter and discuss it with them.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO ASSISTANCE IN DRY AREAS

speechtext: It might. I was not aware that the United States authorities were allowing these very small craft through their locks, and in view of what the hon. member for Laurier has said I will be glad to discuss the question with the officials of the seaway.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. The meteorological branch is responsible for all phases of meteorological service for civil and military purposes in Canada, for shipping in adjacent ocean areas or on the great lakes, and for

international aviation over the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and polar and subpolar routes. Highlights of new and expanded services provided for in the 1959-60 estimates include:
1.	A comprehensive ice observing and forecasting program in direct support of marine activity in the lower St. Lawrence, gulf of St. Lawrence, Hudson bay and sea supply lines to the far north. The major portion of the ice observing will be accomplished through aerial reconnaissance using chartered aircraft. The cost of that amounts to $400,000.
2.	Extension of meteorological research particularly, in the fields of atmospheric ozone, radiation, turbulence, cloud physics and in the determination of the relationships of meteorological factors applicable to agriculture, forestry and so forth, $134,000.
3.	Development of forecasting techniques and extension of services on a routine basis for high level jet aircraft operations, $100,000.
4.	Development and testing of methods of preparing weather forecast charts at various levels of the atmosphere by purely numerical means using high-speed electronic computers, $90,000.
5.	Replacement of departmentally owned radio communications facilities by commercial services for the collection and dissemination of meteorological information at such locations as White Horse, Churchill and Goose. Hitherto such commercial facilities have not been available. The cost of that is $216,000.
6.	Establishment of two additional local forecast offices to serve aviation and industrial agencies and the general public in the Fredericton and Quebec city areas, $30,000.
7.	Operation of surface observing stations at cape Dyer, Northwest Territories, and cape Parry, Northwest Territories, and of an upper air station at Goose, Labrador. These are now staffed by United States agencies; $140,000.
A continuing shortage of professional personnel continues to seriously restrict the capabilities of the branch in meeting the ever-increasing demands for service to continuously expanding fields of endeavour. All other items which have not been specified account for $327,000.

The present arrangement under which the majority of airports are federally operated, particularly in the secondary field category, is the result of historical development and wartime growth. I hope hon. members to the right will take it in the objective nature that it is being suggested. I raise this in connection with the Vancouver international airport. There were expropriations filed in 1954 and at that time the vast majority of the cases were settled.
What I wish to draw to the attention of the minister is that under the expropriation Act and also the Exchequer Court Act, unfortunately the valuation of the property has to be made at the date of expropriation. I feel that some consideration should be given to reviewing present expropriation procedures

Supply-Transport
because, under conditions as we have them today, property valuations have been increasing over the years. However, under the present system of expropriation a person is entitled only to the valuation of the property on the date of expropriation which, in this particular instance, is 1954, plus possibly an allowance of 10 per cent for forcible taking.
I lay no blame on the Department of Transport or on the particular people involved, but sometimes these properties are expropriated with extremely long range plans in view. It has been the practice, very often, to allow the people to remain in possession of these properties, without any settlement being effected. The result has been that when the time for settlement comes around the settlement is made on the basis of 1954 valuations. I have had a great deal of difficulty, personally, explaining to these people why they cannot get the advantage of the increased value. I would suggest that the minister give consideration to a plan whereby, for example, if property has been expropriated and no settlement has been made within one year, some provision could be made so that the owner could take advantage of increased land values. If that is not possible, then perhaps the replacement value of the property could be used as a basis for settlement so the person could locate in a similar place under similar circumstances.
As a result of having been associated with some of these individuals I suspect the minister's answer might be that they could proceed in the exchequer court, but the attitude toward people involved in these expropriation proceedings has been to load the gun in favour of the department. The majority of these people with small holdings are unable to afford the cost of expropriation proceedings. I feel some consideration should be given to reviewing the Expropriation Act and the Exchequer Court Act to provide for some of these contingencies in the future.

subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Peters for the second reading of Bill No. C-8, to provide for minimum wages for employees.

subtopic: PROVISION OF MINIMUM RATE OF WAGES FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate adjourned on February 27 I had just risen to make a few comments on this bill. Perhaps, to refresh our memories, I should refer to the explanatory note of the bill. It says:
The purpose of this bill is to establish a minimum rate of wages with respect to all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction. This bill provides that such minimum rate of wages shall be $1.25 per hour. The bill also provides that its terms do not affect any employee whose rate of wages is higher than the minimum established

Industrial Relations
by this legislation. However, any rate of wages less favourable to employees than $1.25 per hour is superseded by this bill.
The last time this was discussed I had expressed approval of the principle of a minimum wage law. I was about to differ with the principle of this bill, and I think that one of the main objections to it lies in the fact that it says that this bill can apply only to those who come under federal jurisdiction. 1 believe that to be a serious defect in the bill and I believe it would nullify the value that it would have otherwise. The second objection I take to it is that $1.25 an hour may be suitable in one part of the country; it may be too low in another pari and it may be too high in still another part of the country.
I should like now to refer to one matter which the member for Timiskaming mentioned when he introduced the bill. He compared it with a previous minimum wage bill which had been introduced in 1935 and was actually enacted by the parliament of Canada. That bill, of course, did differ greatly from the present one inasmuch as its purpose was to apply to everyone in Canada, not only to those under federal jurisdiction. This is a matter that seems to come up quite often these days. When we come to enact legislation we find a conflict of jurisdiction between the federal and provincial governments.
I think nearly everybody who took part in the debate of that day did refer to the fact that this legislation had been referred to the Supreme Court of Canada which ruled it to be ultra vires. I must confess that at the time this was last discussed I felt that was the case myself. However, I have before me the page of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada at that time and I believe this has a very important bearing on all of our labour legislation.
It has been suggested many times that we should have uniform labour legislation and, of course, the purpose of the bill in 1935 was to ratify one of the conventions of the international labour organization which had been set up pursuant to the treaty of Versailles and under the auspices of the League of Nations. We are still members of that international labour organization, and we have not been able to ratify many of the conventions of that organization because of this very conflict that arose over the jurisdiction of federal and provincial governments.
I should like to refer to the judgment of the supreme court at that time, because as it turns out the legislation was not found to be ultra vires by the supreme court. Three of the justices held that it was intra vires
[Mr. Browne (Vancouver-Kingsway) .3
of the federal government and three justices held that it was ultra vires. As a result, it was referred it to privy council who then declared that it was ultra vires. Of course, we are not faced with that situation today. If the same decision had to be made over again it would be the Supreme Court of Canada who would have the decision to make and for that reason I think it is very interesting to look at the decision that was made by the supreme court at that time. I am just going to refer to it now.
I hold in my hand a book from the library of parliament entitled "Supreme Court and Privy Council Judgments Special Legislation-1934-1935". This is in the matter of a reference as to whether the parliament of Canada had legislative jurisdiction to enact the Weekly Rest in Industrial Undertakings Act, being chapter 14 of the Statutes of Canada, 1935; the Minimum Wages Act, being chapter 44 of the Statutes of Canada, 1935; and the Limitation of Hours of Work Act, being chapter 63 of the Statutes of Canada, 1935. There was a good deal of other social legislation enacted by the Bennett government at that time and the other acts that were passed at that time were ruled ultra vires by the supreme court. However, in this case, as I pointed out, there were three judges on each side. This is the head note:
Held, per Duff C. J. and Davis and Kerwin J. J.. that these acts are intra vires of the parliament of Canada; per Rinfret, Cannon and Crocket J. J., that they are ultra vires.
I should like to read a portion of the judgment of the three judges who held that it was intra vires of the federal government.
From two main considerations, the conclusion follows that legislative authority in respect of international agreements is, as regards Canada, vested exclusively in the parliament of Canada. First, by virtue of section 132 of the British North America Act, jurisdiction, legislative and executive, for the purpose of giving effect to any treaty obligation imposed upon Canada, or any one of the provinces of Canada, by force of a treaty between the British Empire and a foreign country, is committed to the parliament and government of Canada. This jurisdiction of the dominion the privy council held, in the Aeronautics case and in the Radio case is exclusive; and consequently, under the British North America Act, the provinces have no power and never had power to legislate for the purpose of giving effect to an international agreement: that, as a subject of legislation, is excluded from the jurisdiction envisaged by section 92.
Second, as a result of the constitutional development of the last 30 years, and more particularly of the last 20 years, Canada has acquired the status of an international unit, that is to say, she has been recognized by His Majesty the King, by the other nations of the British commonwealth of nations, and by the nations of the world, as possessing a status enabling her to enter into, on her own behalf, international arrangements, and to incur obligations under such arrangements. These arrangements may take various forms. They may take the form of treaties, in the strict sense, between heads of states.

to which His Majesty the King is formally a party. They may take, inter alia, the form of agreements between governments, in which His Majesty does not formally appear, Canada being represented by the governor general in council or by a delegate or delegates authorized directly by him. Whatever the form of the agreement, it is now settled that, as regards Canada, it is the Canadian government acting on its own responsibility to the parliament of Canada which deals with the matter. If the international contract is in the form of a treaty between heads of states, His Majesty acts, as regards Canada, on the advice of his Canadian government.
It goes on with two or three further instances and I will refer to one particularly farther down the page. It says:
-in all these matters the authority of parliament in not merely paramount but exclusive.
The Minister of Labour was asked a question in the house a few days ago with respect to why we had not ratified some of the conventions of the international labour organization. I believe this is a matter worth pursuing and if we can find some way of enacting legislation that will apply to the whole country I think it would be very worth while. However, in view of the fact that the bill would only apply to those who come under federal jurisdiction, as it exists at the present time I am sure everyone will agree that the bill is not suitable.
The hon. member who introduced the bill placed on Hansard information as to the minimum wage provisions of the various provinces. We find that the amounts range from a low of 35 cents per hour in Newfoundland to a high of 75 cents per hour in British Columbia. It would seem to me to be absolutely ridiculous to have legislation providing for a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour which would apply to employees of federal organizations in a province and at the same time a provincial statute making provision for a minimum wage of only 35 cents an hour. It would be completely discriminatory in the case of firms that came under federal jurisdiction.
I think that emphasizes the other point I have made that from the range of minimum wage rates in the various provinces across Canada we can see that one minimum wage might not be suitable and if federal legislation were enacted applying to the whole country that would not mean that there would not have to be varying rates. Certainly that was taken into consideration in the original legislation enacted in 1935. Provision was made for varying rates across the country if that was found to be necessary, and I firmly believe that is the case. Therefore for the reasons I have mentioned I strongly suggest that this measure be rejected at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to say how very privileged I am to have the opportunity of speaking on such an important measure as minimum wages, the subject before the house at this time. I should also like to take this opportunity to commend most heartily the hon. member who has brought this legislation before the house because I feel that I am not alone and that in fact every hon. member of the house is against the possibility of any one Canadian or any group of Canadians, any one labourer or group of labourers, being exploited as a cheap labour source. This, sir, is intolerable. In fact, one of the principles of the bill is concerned with protecting people against such exploitation. As the hon. member who has just spoken has so well pointed out, our ability as a federal legislative body is limited with regard to minimum wages, but I believe that every member of the house is definitely against those conditions which permit the exploiting of a cheap labour source.
Before I go into the actual merits of the bill I want to touch very briefly on something I have noticed during private member's hours. There seems to be an attitude that once such bills are presented by hon. members opposite there is an attempt to talk them out. I do not want to go on the defensive or make excuses but I should like to state in the most forthright and sincere manner that invariably bills presented to the House of Commons during this hour are of a contentious or complicated nature and require sincere and close study by all members of the house. For my part I should simply like to state that I do not think there is political cowardice involved in any sense whatsoever when I say I am not prepared to vote on this bill at the present time.
I do not suggest that this legislation should be shelved but it needs objective study and I feel that the discussion during private members' hours helps to contribute to the gathering of material which in turn will help to contribute to good legislation that will stamp out the ability of any employer to exploit a cheap labour source. Let us look at clause three of the bill. As has been pointed out time and again by previous speakers, clause three provides as follows:
This act applies to and in respect of employment upon or in connection with any work, undertaking or business that is within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, including, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing-
As has been pointed out, our ability to be very effective in a legislative way with regard to minimum wages is restricted here.

Industrial Relations
I say this because I think it is most important that after the debate is over no member of the House of Commons should try to go out and say to the public that what is involved is legislation to provide a minimum wage of $1.25 right across the board for all types of work in all areas of Canada from coast to coast. That is just not the case.
Before preparing my notes for this debate I talked at length with officials of the Department of Labour and I am sincerely satisfied that the question of minimum wage legislation-I know this is an often used expression-is receiving active and thorough consideration by the Department of Labour. I think that a definition of minimum wage is something that we should try to arrive at in our discussion of the subject. Historically the definition of minimum wage in by-gone days was a living wage. Later minimum wages were described in relation to varying standards of living. At the international labour organization conference in 1928 minimum wage was described as a suitable standard of living.
Within the provincial sphere we find that during the past years the provinces have tended to define a minimum wage as a wage sufficient to cover the cost of living. This has been arrived at by preparing a list of commodities necessary for a worker and his family to be able to live in a suitable manner. Herein lies a very important attempt to define exactly what we mean by a minimum wage. We know that a minimum wage for skilled labour is often arrived at by collective agreement brought about by union activity. This is done under the collective agreements act in the province of Quebec and, in the other provinces, under the industrial standards act. In fact I think it is most important that we point out right now that because of the conditions to which the hon. member who has just spoken referred, because of varying local conditions right across the nation, I feel it is important that union activity, not always but largely union activity, brings about the necessary minimum wage levels.
It is becoming increasingly apparent across the country that it is the unions who, by their responsible actions, are bringing about at least what we should call minimum wages for the workers under their jurisdiction. It was pointed out how difficult it is, even within a province, to arrive at uniform minimum wage legislation. Zones have to be set up between industrial and rural areas. As the hon. member who has just spoken pointed out, in most provinces the minimum wage is different from the amount that we are now discussing in this chamber.
Another thing that comes to my mind in looking over the proposed measure-I can be

corrected if I am wrong-is that so far as I can ascertain this is the first time that the federal parliament has attempted to deal with the problem of minimum wages by statute. In the past it has seemed wiser not to deal with minimum wages per se by statute. Naturally, with the experience of the past before us I am led to wonder if certain risks are not involved in dealing with minimum wages by statute. We see that in those specific provinces which I have already mentioned there are minimum wages fixed by minimum wage boards.
Before closing, there is one thing that I do want to stress most emphatically, and it is this: We are not hiding anything, but this is definitely a matter of considerable importance to the labouring force. I believe the Progressive Conservative party has shown what its attitude toward the workers of this country is since we came to power. We have the contemplated amendments to the unemployment insurance legislation before us. The Minister of Labour has actively placed great emphasis on the national placement service of the Department of Labour. During the last session we saw the Minister of Labour introduce legislation to extend the unemployment insurance benefits. Now the company is in effect attempting to transfer its loss to the residents of these areas, because elimination of trains would reduce the capital value of property in the communities now served.
We have no copy of the agreement between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the dominion government, but are advised that it is a term of that agreement that the company would build a line from Winnipeg to Edmonton and maintain

service thereon as a condition of obtaining land grants from the dominion government. If such is the case, it would seem to us that on this ground alone the application should be refused.
I am not personally acquainted with Mr. N. R. Crump, the president of the Canadian Pacific railway, but from all I hear he is a great Canadian, a great railroad man and, I believe, is the peer of any of those who preceded him in the office of president of the C.P.R. I have no doubt that while I am only a silent partner in his great organization- I think all that I own in the C.P.R. would probably cover the cost of a couple of rails and maybe a few ties-nevertheless as one of the silent partners I would urge him to continue the service on that line. I hope that the Minister of Transport will use some of the eloquence and persuasiveness-and he convinced me yesterday that he is both eloquent and persuasive-to persuade the C.P.R. to continue that service. I want to assure him right now that there are thousands of people in the north end of the constituency of Kindersley who will rise up and call his name blessed if he keeps that line open.

Mr. Chairman, trains No. 41 and 42 are the ones that the hon. member has been referring to. The application is now under investigation by the board's inspectors and I am advised that it will likely come to hearing in September. I shall be very glad to bring the representations of the hon. member to the attention of Mr. Crump.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Has this item anything to do with the painting of box cars as a safety factor? I have not seen any box cars so far that have been painted and I am wondering how many have been done and what is the extent of the project.
The judgment directing the railways to carry this out was issued two months ago and there really has not been time to put it into operation yet but I am sure it will be soon.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I should like to point out that there is some urgency involved. Two or three weeks ago a car with a number of young people in it ran into the side of a freight train in my constituency and they were all very badly injured. The train was very long and they came up to the level crossing and did not see it. I should like to see this work proceeded with as quickly as possible because quite a number of such accidents are taking place, many of them fatal. I think this move would be of help in avoiding some of these accidents.
We are urging the railways to get on with the work as quickly as possible and we will keep right after them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I understand there is some problem with respect to United States railway box cars. As a large number of United States box cars are hauled by Canadian railways, there is a question of what the result will be if the Canadian railways do it and the United States railways do not. I understood there was some discussion with relation to the use of United States box cars that might not be so protected.
As the hon. member probably knows, the railways objected to this but the board has ordered them to go ahead and paint these signs on all new cars and an equal number of old cars.

I understand that an order has been issued that all box cars produced and used in Canada must have these reflectors on them but has Canada any authority to demand that all United States box cars coming into Canada shall be equipped in the same manner?
All new box cars are having these reflectors put on them and all old box cars as they come into the shops.
I am sorry, the minister did not understand.
No, we do not have authority over United States cars coming into the country.

That is an interesting point. Do you mean to tell me that the government

Supply-Transport
of Canada cannot issue instructions that no foreign box car shall come on Canadian soil unless it complies with Canadian law, provided our act is amended?
I am advised we have no authority to do that.
Well, we are not a sovereign state any longer.

In view of the fact that this order has been introduced for the safety of Canadian citizens, may I ask whether any approach has been or is being made to the United States railway companies to ask that a similar policy be followed there with respect to cars coming into Canada? Has any approach been made?
I am advised this would require legislation by the United States and that a number of bills have been introduced in congress in the past and none of them has passed yet.

We have the authority to pass any legislation we wish in this chamber. If we amended the act would that not be sufficient to cause United States cars coming into Canada to be equipped in compliance with the law?
The main objection would be that this would completely interrupt transborder trade. It would be very detrimental to trade across the border.

I understand the explanation of the minister but in view of the fact that it is now mandatory with respect to all Canadian box cars will the minister endeavour to have the Department of External Affairs make it known that this is now the law in Canada and ask whether it is possible for United States box cars to be so equipped so that they will comply with our Canadian law?
Yes, we will do that.

speechtext: May I ask the minister what is the present state of the Canadian ocean going fleet? I should like to know how many vessels were under the Canadian flag a year ago and how many are under the Canadian flag now.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask what action, if any, the minister or the government have taken in the last year to stem the decline of the Canadian merchant fleet?

Mr. Chairman, we have been no more able to stem the decline of the Canadian merchant fleet than was the former government. I have some figures here that I know will interest the hon. member and the committee. The total number of deep sea ships under Canadian registry in 1946 was 151. By 1956, when the former government was still in office, this number had shrunk to 26 and as of March 31 of this year, the number was 13. I think the hon. member and the committee will realize that this is a continuing process and that it appears no government is able to do very much about it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister did not answer my question. 1 simply asked the minister what action the government has taken to stem the reduction. If he wants to make a comparison, he said himself that there were 151 in 1946 and this number had declined to 26. Now, this number has been cut in half. My question, which the minister did not answer when he said that no more was done than before, is, what has been done by the present administration to stem the decline of the Canadian merchant fleet?
Mr. Chairman, the decline has largely taken place as a result of the sale of old ships. There has been some replacement, but not very much.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

As the hon. member knows, being pretty good at arithmetic, the eight ships-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Has the minister or the government given any consideration to giving Canadians engaged in this field of enterprise any tax reductions such as was done by the introduction of legislation for depreciation two years ago, I believe?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is another matter which I should like to bring to the minister's attention, and it is this: A large part of the present Canadian ocean-going fleet consists of vessels built during the war which are no longer competitive with vessels from other countries.
