speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wish to bring a matter to the attention of the minister, and it is one which would have been brought up by the hon. member for Levis, had he been here. It has to do with a steamship subsidy which was paid by the maritime commission under the jurisdiction of the department for a service operating between Isle aux Grues and Mont-magny. It seems to be a most unfortunate situation because a ferry operator who had been running this service for a period of 30 years, and who had been receiving a subsidy for the last 10 years of $3,300 for summer service, $1,700 for winter service, plus $1,000 per year from the postal department, now finds himself without the subsidy at all. In other words, from the information the hon. member for Levis has given me and which I now have before me, it looks as if the department simply cut this man off without giving him the slightest notice. This action was taken with regard to a man who had been operating the service for 30 years.
I should like to put on the record a paragraph from the file that was left with me by the hon. member for Levis:
(Translation):
For close to 30 years, Mr. Gagne has been carrying mail between the lie aux Grues and Montmagny. Last year, he received $1,000 for this service. In addition to his postal duties, Mr. Gagne operated a freight and passenger water transport service between those two points. The service has been subsidized for nearly 10 years by the Canadian Maritime Commission on the following basis: $3,300 for the summer service, $1,700 for the winter service. It was this grant that enabled him to carry the mail for a price of $1,000 a year.
On March 2, Mr. Gagne received from the Canadian Maritime Commission, a letter,-of which I enclose a copy-informing him that his grant would not be renewed, on the grounds that a bigger ship was required for that service. Never before that letter had the commission asked Mr. Gagne to operate a larger ship.
(Text):
I have a letter in my possession which was written by the director of steamship subvention service in answer to a letter from the operator, Mr. Gagne, dated December 30 and sent to him on March 2, almost three months later, saying that his contract had been cancelled and that he was simply out of luck. It seems to me that if these circumstances are correct it was a most unfair way in which to deal with a man who had been operating this service for 30 years. What is more, it seems to me that the first thing that should have been done at least should have been to

Supply-Transport
offer to give this man an opportunity to perform the new service at the same or similar conditions which were available to other tenderers. Frankly, I feel, and the hon. member for Levis feels, very strongly about this. I think an injustice has been done to this man.

Mr. Chairman, the Mr. Gagne to whom the hon. member refers has been carrying on this service for a number of years with a small ship incapable of carrying automobiles or farm machinery. Early this year a Mr. Lavoie offered to undertake the service with a ship capable of carrying automobiles and tractors. On March 2 the maritime commission wrote to Mr. Gagne advising him of the situation and telling him that in view of the greater suitability of Mr. Lavoie's vessel his contract would not be renewed. This was two months before the commencement of the service. It is true that the delay was short. But the other offer had only been received recently and there was little time to examine it.
The commission has always tried to award these services locally when possible. In this case both the former contractor and the present contractor are from the area. On March 19, Mr. Gagne, the former contractor acknowledged the commission's letter, and although he expressed disappointment at the short notice and award of the contract to another, he made no mention of his ability to supply a larger vessel.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why was he not given the opportunity to supply the ship, as it has been the practice of the maritime commission over a number of years?

If he had come forward with a ship of comparable size and performance with that of Mr. Lavoie undoubtedly he would have been given the contract. It was well known that he did not have such a ship, that he had only the one ship and was unable to perform the service. Therefore in the interests of the people who would be served by this ferry, the better and more capable ship was being used.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why was he not given a chance to submit a tender on the newer ship?
This was no secret to his fellow islanders. They knew all about this. This matter was well known down there and was discussed by them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the minister answer my question?
He had the opportunity. He knew two months before. If he had come forward with a comparable ship he certainly would have been given every opportunity to tender but he did not do so.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, those are not the facts. The facts are that when the time arrived for the new service to be entered upon this man was not given an opportunity to tender. The circumstances and the facts are to that effect. The minister confirms that situation in his reply now because it has been the practice of the maritime commission, when a service like this is brought to an end to give to the former operator an opportunity of tendering on the new appliances.

As I have said, it was well known that this gentleman, Mr. Gagne, did not have a suitable ship. If he had had a suitable ship he would certainly have had every opportunity. When he was notified two months before the termination of the contract, if he had come forward and said, "I can produce a better type of ship that can perform the service that is needed by the residents of this area", he would then, of course, have been given every opportunity to tender. But he did not do so. It was well known by all concerned that he did not have a ship. I do not think the hon. member would wish the people of the area to put up with inferior service when a far better service is available to them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister is just a little bit too suave in this case to be able to get around the circumstances. I can tell the minister exactly what happened. The point is that the new incumbent is a strong supporter of the minister's administration.
What is wrong with that?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is this the matter with it. The other man should have been given an opportunity to submit a tender, particularly when he had been operating the service for 30 years.
It serves him right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hear that interruption which came from down at the other end of the chamber and which was to the effect that it served him right. If that is the kind of policy we are going to have from hon. gentlemen opposite-"it serves them right because they voted Liberal"-it is a good thing to know and a good thing to have on the record. I submit here that this policy is not the kind of policy that should be followed by any department or by any government. A man who has been providing a service such as this should at least have been given the opportunity to tender on the new requirements for the service. Furthermore I am told that the population on the island has decreased somewhat and that therefore it may be quite doubtful whether a larger ship was required. I think the minister owes this committee an explanation.

I can say this very clearly. Political considerations had no effect whatsoever and did not come into this matter in the slightest degree. This man was given a contract on one basis and one basis only, namely that he could provide a far better service for the same subsidy. It seems to me to be a little bit strange that not so long ago in relation to some debate hon. members opposite were protesting or suggesting the waste of government money. Here, with the same subsidy, we can get for the people of that area a far superior ferry service. But the hon. member is suggesting that for the same subsidy that this government pays we should put up with inferior service.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not suggest that.
That is exactly what you are suggesting.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I will not let the minister put those words in my mouth. I am not suggesting that at all. I am trying to get at the difficulty.
I have nothing to get at. There is no difficulty as far as I am concerned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The point is this. You are talking about a new service.
Address the Chair.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Why did you not give this man an opportunity to tender?

That man had every opportunity if he had had a sufficiently good ship to support his tender. He knew two months before the new operation started. He was not so shy or so backward as all that. If he had wanted to do so or felt that he had a ship that could perform the services required he could have written us and said, "I have a ship as good as that myself and for that subsidy I will provide as good a service", and of course he would have been given every opportunity. That is the way in which this government treats people; if they come forward with a reasonable proposition they are welcomed with open arms. What we are aiming at is to give the people in every constituency of Canada the very best value possible for their tax dollar and that is what we intend to do. We do not intend to force upon them an inferior service which perhaps had been done for quite some time by the former government because perhaps this man, Gagne, was a supporter of the former government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
You must have thought that he was fairly good because you carried him for two years after the former government left office. You must have thought his services were satisfactory. However, I want to
Supply-Transport
draw to your attention the manner in which this contract was brought to an end. I should like to put on the record the letter which came from the director of subvention services. It is addressed to Mr. Gagne and is dated March 2, 1959, three months after the operator of this service had written to the director of subvention services. It reads as follows:
(Translation):
Dear Mr. Gagne,
I acknowledge your letter of February 21 concerning your application, dated December 30, 1958, for renewal of your subsidy contract.
I regret the delay that has occurred, but the commission has been conducting a general inquiry into representations it had received for the provision of a larger ship which would allow automobiles and self-propelled agricultural machinery to be transported to the island through the regular service at a reasonable cost, and would avoid the necessity of hiring a special ship for such purposes, at heavy expense.
The commission has reviewed all aspects of the matter and has decided that the . . .
(Text):
I cannot make out the name of the ship. (Translation):
-is not suitable in the circumstances. I am therefore directed to inform you that your contract will not be renewed in 1959.
The contract has been awarded to Captain Eugene Lavoie, who operates the-
(Text):
Then again it is the name of the ship that I cannot make out. I think it is St. Jacques. (Translation):
I regret this situation, which arises from the increasing number of machines and vehicles on the island, and from the necessity of providing for their transportation.
I therefore take this opportunity to thank you, on behalf of the commission, for your co-operation in the past years.
Yours sincerely, etc.,
(Text):
It is quite clearly set out here that the man had not the slighest opportunity to tender on these new services that the minister, now that his government is in office, wants to give to the people in the area. After all, it seems to me that the man who had been there for so long should at least have been given an opportunity. He was not given an opportunity because he was a Liberal.

That is not the case at all. If it was known that the man had a suitable ship he would have been given every opportunity. In communities like that everybody knows fairly well what everybody else has. It was well known that this man had one ship and not one of satisfactory size and capacity. If he had come forward and said, "I should like to have the privilege of tendering" he certainly would have been given it. We are simply carrying out in this instance our policy of

Supply-Transport
providing the best services for the people in every riding in Canada at the lowest cost to the taxpayer.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister a question which I think I should have asked on the previous item, but I know I will be at least 51 per cent or more in order because it is related to ships' equipment. The people of Canada, at least those who are used to using our waters, are very interested in the design of a satisfactory lifesaving vest for use on small craft. I understand the minister called a conference in connection with this matter last year, and I wonder if he could report to the house what progress has been made by his department with respect to designing a satisfactory lifesaving vest for use by people in small watercraft.

Yes, Mr. Chairman. We have had several meetings with the manufacturers and users. Improved designs have been submitted and are being examined at the present time, and we consider that satisfactory progress is being made toward this very desirable end.

Mr. Chairman, I am intrigued by this peculiar approach that the Department of Transport has down in this locale where everybody knows everybody else. It seems to me that is a most peculiar basis for operating or changing any services. I know how distinguished these services are because the minister has reiterated a number of times that they give the best possible service at the lowest possible cost, and everybody knows everybody else. What is this principle of everybody knowing everybody else? Can the minister explain how large a community would get before you decide that everybody does not know everybody else and that maybe you could have a bid or a tender, or maybe a public announcement inviting tenders. I would like to know whether Port Arthur and Fort William are the sort of communities where everybody knows everybody else. How does the minister manage to appoint somebody up there who happens to be a brother-in-law of a local Conservative politician?

Mr. Chairman, to start off with, everybody is somebody or other's brother-in-law, and the fortunate ones have Conservatives as brothers-in-law. That shows they have good judgment and have married into the right kind of family. As to the size of communities where everybody knows everybody else, I would not think for a moment that in Fort William or Port Arthur people would, because they are very big, important and imposing cities and people do not know everybody else. That is the case in large and

important cities such as those. But I had the privilege last fall of visiting Isle aux Grues and I visited a great many families there and found them extremely charming and delightful, and I can assure the hon. member that in a friendly community like Isle aux Grues everybody knows everybody else and they are very informed on matters of this kind.

Mr. Chairman, under the details of this item for steamship services on the west coast, the western local services, one of them is Vancouver and northern British Columbia ports, in the amount of $194,500, and the other is the Vancouver and west coast of Vancouver island service, $100,-
000.	I wonder if the minister can tell me what companies are involved in these subsidies, what ships they provide for the service and the ports of call that they must make?
The company is the Northland Navigation Company and the ships are the Canadian Prince and the Tahsis Prince.
Which ship, Mr. Chairman, operates on the west coast of Vancouver island?
The Tahsis Prince.
I take it that is a new ship which has gone on that run?
Yes, that is correct.

I would like to make a suggestion, although I rather hesitate to do it, about the comparison between the British Columbia coast and the Atlantic coast and the amount of the subventions, because I think there is perhaps the possibility of saving a little money on the Pacific coast. I would like to ask the minister if he has ever given any consideration to initiating a service on the west coast to the island from Port Alberni? I believe it could be done and would give a much more frequent and better service for less money.
I am told this has been considered, Mr. Chairman, but it was considered impractical because nearly all the freight originates in Vancouver.

Mr. Chairman, that is
hardly an answer. I happen to know that part of the country very well. Perhaps a great deal of it does originate in Vancouver, but it comes to Port Alberni and is transferred to ships already going down to the other end of Barkley sound so there would be no difficulty in transferring freight into ships going to Nootka and Kyuquot. I hope the minister will also take that out of his serious consideration basket and put it in his urgent basket.
Yes, I shall be glad to.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to again bring to the attention of the minister the need of the people of Grand Manan for increased transportation facilities. I realize that is not the direct responsibility of the minister's department, but included in this item is an amount of $95,000 which is a subsidy paid annually to the Grand Manan ferry. Grand Manan is an island in the bay of Fundy, having a population of about 2,600 people, and I would like to put on record part of the brief submitted by the people of Grand Manan and the board of trade to the provincial government:
As expressed in the text of this petition, the present service when inaugurated in 1946 was at the time classified as a service of temporary nature, subject to improvement when a more suitable vessel could be obtained, and this information would be on file in Ottawa.
When the previous transportation system was set up in 1930 it consisted of a newly built ferry especially constructed to meet the requirements of this particular service, in which there was accommodation for 12 automobiles carried underdeck, a freight compartment adequate to service this area, and comfortable passenger accommodations for slightly over one hundred people.
During the years 1930 and 1939 the tourist traffic to Grand Manan showed yearly increase, there was an increase in the number of inns catering to this trade, and expansion programs were undertaken by the already established hostelries.
This ferry service was taken over in 1939 and a converted private yacht put on in 1946. This yacht can only handle nine passenger cars and these are put on with a derrick and must remain on deck. There is a most inadequate freight service and the accommodation is limited to about 20 people. Now the island of Grand Manan, as members of this committee know, is essentially a fish producing area, but in order to ship the fish to the mainland and maintain supplies it must have adequate contact with the mainland by ferry. It is the wish of the people of the island that they be provided with a ferry capable of handling below deck 30 cars and having a reasonable accommodation for passengers. I suggest to the minister that he and the officials of his department should take another look at this question to see whether the subsidy paid by the federal treasury cannot be utilized to supply the people of this island with an adequate ferry service to keep them in contact with the province of New Brunswick.
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

On this item, which I think is a very important item because it deals with the national harbours board, I wish to make one suggestion in particular to the minister, and though this board is, of course, of importance right across Canada, I wish to speak only of its operations as they affect a certain area in British Columbia.
I am sure that all hon. members from the lower mainland of British Columbia, irrespective of party, are keenly interested in and perhaps a little worried about the situation regarding the development on the Fraser river. To the best of my knowledge there are now in the Fraser river area two harbour commissions. We have a harbour commission in New Westminster and we have a harbour commission on the north Fraser.
The Fraser river has played a most important and integral part in the economy of British Columbia. The lower mainland has developed at a very rapid rate, and because of that I personally believe that we have now reached a point when a new look should be taken at the development of the Fraser river and an endeavour made to bring in not only the city of New Westminster but all the adjoining municipalities which have a vital interest in that area. I know from my own studies in the past that the harbour board in New Westminster has had a fairly free hand, but New Westminster as such is now pretty well developed with regard to harbour facilities, and with the growth on the Fraser river of the adjoining municipalities I would dare to guess that inside a very few years the adjoining municipalities will equal, if not surpass, the city of New Westminster in population. But up till now there has been very little interest, if any, in development on the other side of the river and in the upstream and downstream areas.
I know from my personal knowledge that a few years ago this was recognized by the harbour commission in New Westminster, and the commission endeavoured to work out a plan whereby they would have control. That plan failed. The result is that at the present

Supply-Transport
time an endeavour is being made, perhaps without the knowledge of the minister, to tie in the north Fraser harbour commission with the commission in New Westminster. Who instigated this move, I do not know. I have received a great number of letters protesting any such idea. I do know from my own personal discussions with the Minister of Transport that he himself is not a party to this proposal. However, I would draw the attention of the Minister of Transport to the fact that this matter of harbour commissions on the Fraser river is one which I understand includes the activities of his own department, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Public Works and, I believe, one or two others. Honestly, I am afraid there has not been coordination and co-operation between the various departments of government relative to the development of the Fraser river as far as it is concerned as a navigable river up to a certain point and also involving the question of agriculture and of fisheries.
The Fraser river is, as I have said, a most important economic factor in the life of British Columbia, especially on the lower mainland where almost half of the population of British Columbia is concentrated. I firmly believe the time has come when there must be major planning to deal with the problems of the Fraser river and a co-ordinated effort by all the departments of government concerned. The Minister of Transport has, I believe, the major responsibility because the matter comes under his estimates. I should like to ask the minister if he will say whether there is any realization in his department and in the various departments themselves that the time has come to establish a Fraser river control board or commission so as to bring in all the rapidly growing municipalities, such as Burnaby, Port Coquitlam, Port Moody and the others up the river. I am certain that I am not breaking any confidence when I say that I discussed one angle with the minister relative to what is now the understanding by a great many people and organizations on the lower mainland that there is a drive to have the north Fraser harbour commission swallowed up by amalgamation with New Westminster.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Would the hon. member mind if I finished and then I shall be glad to answer his question.

It is right on the particular point he is now making. The hon. member keeps referring to this proposed amalgama-

tion. I was wondering whether he could inform us as to what is the basis of his information?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I will be glad to. The basis of my information is the minutes of a recent meeting of the Burnaby council where the matter was discussed. The basis of my information is the number of letters that I have received from tugboat operators and other commercial firms operating on the north arm of the Fraser river. The basis of my statement is the statement made on June 5 in this House of Commons by the house leader, which is to be found at page 4386 of Hansard, in which the house leader said:
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam advocated the establishment of a Fraser river authority to supervise the development of that great river. An attempt is being made to further the co-operation of the different bodies involved with the river but at the moment there is no plan for an overriding authority. That may come eventually but there would be many difficulties to be ironed out before a movement of that kind could be made.
I say in answer to the question of my colleague from British Columbia that on the basis of my information from municipal councils in the lower mainland, my information from the statement of the house leader in the House of Commons and the letters I have received from such men as Captain Lowrey of the Bridge Towing Limited in British Columbia, and others, this matter very definitely is either under consideration or is rumoured as such.
I bring these matters to the attention of the minister not so much because of the possible abolition of the north Fraser harbour commission, though I would hate to see that at the present moment, but to ask the Minister of Transport whether he would do one of two things. Because of the fact so many departments are concerned-I understand that his own department, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Fisheries are concerned-can he say here, not so much for himself but for those who are so vitally interested in the lower mainland of British Columbia, and particularly those on the Fraser river-my own riding boundaries are about two miles from the Fraser river but I have a keen interest- can he give us a picture under this item as to what is the position as regards the north Fraser commission and its relationship to any possible amalgamation. As a matter of fact, I would forgive the minister if he did not answer those questions provided he would give us a picture on the development of the entire Fraser river and a possible tie-in with the proposed establishment of a new board under a new system but still on the same

basis of a harbour commission under which all cities and municipalities and all those interested, namely agriculture, fishing, tugboats and shipping, could have what is now a basic requirement, namely an over-all Fraser river control board. I cannot think of any other term to use but to use a Fraser river control board. Under this, they could have the most efficient development, the most efficient operation from the mouth of the Fraser river up to the end of navigable waters.

Approaches were made to my department with those ideas in mind some time ago. We looked over the whole situation but we are not going ahead with any plans to carry this amalgamation that the hon. member mentioned into effect, and will not do so unless we are approached by the municipalities and the people concerned who express to us a real and considered desire that this should be done. If such a broad board of authority is suggested to us we will be very glad to discuss it with the people who would bring such an idea forward.

May I ask a supplementary question? Did I gather from what the minister said that, as far as his knowledge goes as minister in charge of the harbour commissions, there is no suggestion by himself or his department of an amalgamation of the north Fraser river, nor any wiping out of the present board; but if there is any need or request for a Fraser river control board it must come to him as a request from the municipalities concerned?
That is correct.
On both questions?
That is correct on both questions.
Mr. Chairman, in the first place I think the hon. member for Vancouver East is maybe a year or a year and a half behind the times. In the second place-
I am sorry; one of our members made the suggestion two years ago.

I said that.

I should like to say a few words on the national harbours board as its operations affect the harbour of Vancouver. I have been looking at the 1958 report and I notice that over the last five years receipts and shipments of grain at the port of Vancouver were 1,170 million bushels compared with 1,119 million bushels in the case of Montreal. Montreal, however, has storage capacity about 77 per cent in excess of that of Vancouver and other facilities to a much greater degree. If we look at the figures for 1958 and 1957 we see that in 1958 receipts and shipments at Montreal amounted to 249 million bushels while the figure for Vancouver was 275 million bushels. In 1957 the figures were 172 million bushels for Montreal and 282 million bushels for Vancouver.
Capital expenditures over the last year were $6 million in Vancouver and $17 million in Montreal. I understand from newspaper reports that there will be very heavy capital expenditures for the port of Montreal in the next year or so. I should like to suggest to the national harbours board that they should make a survey of the port of Vancouver to see whether the facilities are adequate to take care properly of the traffic passing through that port at the present time. I think there is need for an over-all look at what they have there because right now I think there should be in the planning stage a major expansion program with regard to facilities.
I should like them to consider an access road all around the harbour which would be

of advantage for lire fighting if we had a major blaze in the harbour area. At the present time you cannot get to half of the sheds because they are cut off by railway tracks that parallel the harbour. Mr. Chairman, may I ask one question so that the attention will not all be on Vancouver?
It is the best port in the country.

minister how the survey into silting and mud in Saint John harbour, conducted in cooperation with the Department of Public Works and completed a short while ago, is coming along? We are looking forward to the results.

482. Loans to the St. Lawrence seaway authority in such manner and subject to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve. $30,000,000.

This item deals with the St. Lawrence seaway and is for loans to the St. Lawrence seaway authority in such manner and subject to such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve. I believe that due to its misconception and faulty construction this seaway will be like a bottomless pit into which we can sink untold sums of money. I believe that this seaway is obsolete before it is opened. I believe it imperative that before any more money is spent those who constructed it should get full credit for it and assume full responsibility. I believe that there should be a full appreciation of the difficulties which this government will encounter in inheriting the seaway and in trying to make it work.
Since Her Majesty has graciously consented to open the seaway I hope there will be no misunderstanding of what I am saying. I wish to inform the house how eagerly we in Stormont are anticipating the visit to Cornwall of Her Majesty and His Royal Highness on June 27 and how grateful we are to the Prime Minister for his sympathetic understanding of my efforts to include our area in the royal itinerary. Although not a compensation, this is a very gratifying recognition of all the dislocation suffered by the people of this historic seaway valley. It is particularly appropriate as no part of Canada is more loyal and devoted to the crown. In fact, many Stormont people have the unique distinction of belonging to the only civilized races that have never lived under any government but a monarchy. My French Canadian friends escaped the horrors of the French revolution and every Scot is a royalist to the core, especially those whose fathers followed Her Majesty's Stuart ancestors.
From the shores of the St. Lawrence we can still gaze south to the blue haze of the Adirondacks through which winds the Mohawk river on which our great great grandparents turned their backs because they were steadfast to their Tory and loyalist beliefs.
That was well read.

Whatever I, or anyone else, may say of the St. Lawrence seaway, I gladly proclaim that it is the most magnificent engineering feat of modern times. It is the greatest example today of cooperation between two countries which were formerly enemies. It is a symbol of Canada's growing industrial strength and it is, above all, the occasion which warrants the royal visit to our shores. But unfortunately we are so seduced by the idea of size in Canada that if a thing is big enough and costly enough it is unpatriotic or even sacrilegious to criticize it. I do not subscribe to this pagan heresy which is in the same category as Hitler's "big lie". The pyramids of Egypt were also a great engineering feat, but it is questionable whether the glorification of one man was worth all the labour and suffering involved in their construction.
The hundreds of millions of dollars squandered on the Arrow program was due to the megalomania of one man. Yet, think what this money would have done for Canada if it had been spent on the reduction of taxes or to increase old age pensions and family allowances. Think what this increased purchasing power would do to relieve unemployment. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, will the people of Canada have cause in the next 10 years to regard the St. Lawrence seaway as they now regard the Arrow. After the tumult and the shouting dies, after the captains and the Queen depart, I wonder will the whole of Canada awake as disillusioned as Cornwall with the whole seaway project.
In any realistic appraisal of the seaway there are certain basic factors that must be taken into account. The whole pattern of oceanic shipping is changing. The tramp steamer which was willing to pick up a miscellaneous cargo wherever it could be found is being superseded by the liner, either cargo or cargo-passenger, operating on regular schedule. Although a successful liner service is based on high grade traffic, it requires enough low grade bulky freight for ballast. To obtain this it can offer such attractive prices to the shipper that the tramp has difficulty in competing.
A second factor is that ships will have to operate between Montreal and the lake cities at about three-quarters of their normal rate of movement. In addition to the canal, there are about 67 miles of restricted channel in the St. Lawrence with the least width through the Thousand islands from lake Ontario to Chimney point being 500 feet, and about 150 miles of channel navigation from the head of navigation in lake Superior to the head of the St. Lawrence. The passage of each lock takes up to an hour and the river speed of, say 12 miles per hour, would

have to be reduced to about four miles per hour in the canals and about eight miles per hour in the improved channels. In other words, a ship would take over 12 days to make the round trip from Montreal to Duluth, which trip could be performed in 9 days of unrestricted navigation.
Finally, the practical navigation season for ocean vessels is limited to about 6-| months. I know that the average duration of open navigation is 227 days. The average period is roughly from April 26 to December 9. But this is quite different from the practical shipping season.. Boats leaving Montreal for Duluth or Chicago would or must return by the earliest possible closing date at Montreal. It would take 18 days to 20 days to make the trip to Chicago, load, and return. With the date of closing of navigation at Montreal coming sometimes as early as November 25, the last departure could not be later than November 5 or 6. Even this would be cutting it so fine that the insurance rates would naturally be increased substantially. The season for boats going only as far as Detroit would, of course, be about one week longer. This is no problem for the great lake freighters because they can winter in the upper or lower lakes, if necessary.
The economics institute of the Brookings institute, which is supported by the Carnegie trusts, as long ago as 1929 asked most of the major shipping companies of the world whether it would be feasible to operate ships on regular schedules over the St. Lawrence route during the summer months and then lay them up for the winter or shift them to regular services or place them in tramp service during the closed season provided, of course-and this is the biggest proviso-that there were adequate channels and harbour facilities with at least 33 feet draft. Without exception those companies replied that no ocean vessel could obtain sufficient revenue to lay up during the winter season. Deep-sea boats, of course, cannot be used as temporary grain storage elevators as can lakers.
The great majority also answered the later questions in the negative. They pointed out that during the winter months there is no general increase of overseas trade which would enable established trade routes to absorb this additional tonnage, and competition is too keen to let outside tonnage come in and take business away from established lines for part of the year only. Vessels could make a profitable trip to Europe in the same time that they could make the return trip from Montreal to the head of the lake. Regular lines would probably [DOT]confine themselves to ports where they could
Supp ly-Transport
combine cargo with passenger traffic and of course passengers would land and embark as near to the sea as possible rather than take a long, slow inland trip by water.
Most of the shippers also thought that the seaway traffic would not even prove profitable to tramp tonnage. If a tramp vessel contracts to go from Montreal to the head of the lakes for grain, involving a trip of 18 days, she runs the risk of losing a more favourable charter which she might obtain if not tied up with a long inland trip. A small boat of this size could not carry grain from the head of the lakes to Liverpool at a return comparable with that which shippers can obtain via the great lakes bulk freighters to Montreal and large 10,000-ton to 12,000-ton cargo vessels out of Montreal. This small tramp would be less efficient than your great lakes bulk freighters for the inland voyage and less efficient than a first-class cargo liner for the trans-Atlantic run.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make the sober statement that the St. Lawrence seaway as a paying route for ocean vessels is obsolete before it is officially opened. This will sound incredible to many people, I know that the hon. member for Laurier, who conceived the seaway, will vigorously refute this statement. It will probably even be denied by the present Minister of Transport who is left holding the baby. But I make this statement in the firm belief that time and circumstances will prove its validity. It is very interesting, in fact, to note that this statement is substantiated by Mr. B. J. Roberts, Canadian president of the seaway authority who is reported in the Montreal Gazette of May 25, 1959, to have stated, when interviewed on his first tour through the seven locks of the seaway:
From an economic standpoint the use of lakers for bulk cargo may, in the long run, prove to be the best thing for the seaway.
I continue to quote:
The lakers with smaller crews and lower operating expenses can outdo ocean vessels on the seaway and I think they will supersede the larger ships.
He further declared that by running on a light tonnage instead of full capacity the salt water vessels may prove to be uneconomical. I think this is a masterpiece of understatement.
The main reason for this fiasco is the inadequate depth of the seaway for profitable ocean traffic. The question of the appropriate depth was considered by various United States congressional committee in 1951, 1952 and 1953. On February 29, 1952 the Hon. Charles

Supply-Transport
Sawyer, secretary of commerce, testifying before the senate committee on foreign relations stated as follows:
While it is true that only about 10 per cent of the American merchant marine can operate fully loaded in 27 feet of water, the overwhelming part of our merchant fleet-at least 75 per cent-can use the seaway if laden to less than capacity.
It was also stated before the committee that the total additional costs of providing a channel depth of 30 feet upon the unit cost levels of December, 19*50 would have been to the United States, $20,260,000 and to Canada, $23,465,000.
The only justification for the 27-foot depth to have been publicly advanced in Canada is to be found in the following single sentence spoken by the former minister of transport in the House of Commons on December 11, 1951, as reported in Hansard of 1951, second session, at page 1765:
The canal is to be 27 feet deep and that will adequately take care of, I believe it is, very nearly 90 per cent of all the ocean going ships that are in existence at the present time.
In common charity, all that I can say is that the honourable minister, as he then was, must have been including Chinese junks, Portuguese fishing smacks, Jamaican rum schooners and all sorts of other vessels that trade in obscure corners of the world thousands of miles from the St. Lawrence. He must also have included those that could go through empty, but no money is made in that way.
When allowance is made for the lesser buoyance of fresh water and for the squat of a vessel due to forward motion under way, the maximum draft that can be permitted in the seaway is 25 feet. As of December 31, 1957, 978 of the 1,039 vessels in the British merchant fleet-the great proportion of them -are over 25 feet in draft. According to the data supplied by the Canadian maritime commission, which is published in the December, 1957 report of the royal commision on the coasting trade-appendix X, incidentally, pages 261 to 270-it is stated that of Canadian dry cargo vessels of 1,000 gross tons or over, only 10 vessels under Canadian registry and three under United Kingdom registry are under 25.5 feet in draft. The others, 8 under the Canadian flag and 84 under United Kingdom registry, are all over the 25.5 foot limit. Although I shall refrain from doing so, I could itemize the names, tonnages, and drafts of all the Canadian ships.
It must be remembered that the key to profitable shipping is the last two or three inches of cargo in the hold and that an oceangoing ship is a very expensive proposition. Apart from high insurance due to the traditional hazards of inland navigation an

8,000-ton deep sea vessel costs $1,500 a day to operate. In comparison, a laker, because of higher wages, costs $2,000 daily, but it is able to carry 25,000 tons of cargo as opposed to 8,000.
Much of this was pointed out by Dr. C. P. Wright in his excellent book in the St. Lawrence seaway authority, which was published as long ago as 1935, and again in a recent article in the Canadian Banker, which was reprinted in the Montreal Gazette of March 23, 1959, by Mr. Clayton Sinclair. Despite all the ballyhoo about the St. Lawrence seaway, it stands a poor eighth in the size of vessel it will handle in comparison with other great world canals. The Panama canal and the Amsterdam-Rhine canal are 41-feet deep, the Kiel canal is 37 feet, the Suez and Port Arthur, Texas-Beaumont canals, 34 feet, the Houston, Texas, canal 33 feet, and the Manchester ship canal 28 feet. The St. Lawrence seaway will merely be the continent's third largest shipping artery and will not give ocean shipping priority over inland boats like the other two.
Even more fantastic than building an ocean seaway which could not accommodate ocean ships was trying to enter ocean shipping into a Welland canal which was already taxed to capacity. Digging the seaway, while leaving the Welland canal unimproved, was like making a bigger bottle without enlarging the neck. The Montreal Gazette of June 1 of this year commented editorially on the fleet of ships which lay at anchor in lake Ontario waiting to enter the Welland canal as follows: It is, of course, true that the flow of foreign ships into the waterway is partly explained by novelty and experiment. But even when all the abnormal conditions are taken into consideration, it still remains doubtful whether the Welland canal is capable of handling any very remarkable addition to the number of ships it has handled in the past.
Last year it was possible for Canadian ships to pass through the Welland canal in nine hours. This year it is taking up to 58 hours. Not only are the costs of these delays being added to what Canadians must pay, but the level of tolls imposed with the opening of the waterways is yet another addition to the cost structure. The users of iron ore, coal and grain face delays in receiving their supplies-still another addition to costs. The Steel Company of Canada, for example, has already expressed its grave concern at having its supplies held up. If grain cannot be promptly and efficiently shipped through the Welland canal, then there is the possibility that part of the crop is left on the farms. Unless Canadian lake freighters are given priority in the Welland locks the Canadian economy will be seriously injured by the St. Lawrence waterway instead of being:

aided by it; and if Canadian lakers get the necessary priority, the waterway is no longer a seaway.
The hon. member for Laurier has recently published a most interesting book on the St. Lawrence seaway, and despite his modesty it is apparent from his book that more than anyone else in this country or in the United States he was responsible for the conception and the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway. He deserves full credit and full responsibility for this. As I have said, this is a delightful book-
Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order.
-and should make an excellent grade 12 civics text.
Order. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate has risen on a point of order.
Mr. Chairman, now that the hon. member has proved conclusively that the seaway could not be used, could not the minister withdraw the item?

May I continue? Despite the fact that it is such an excellent book, it is not the definitive work that we would expect from a man who took such a leading part in the seaway. Not only will the economists find little there of assistance to them, but even a novice member like myself finds it conspicuously lacking in answers to the questions that concern us here in this house. Why is there no explanation of the monumental disparity between estimated and actual costs? Why were the piers of the south channel bridge at Cornwall not founded on bedrock instead of floating on glacial till, especially when the specification called for them going down to bedrock in view of the fact that a former bridge had collapsed in the same place?
Finally, the whole reason that I am speaking here tonight is to ask, why was the seaway built at all, when it is of little use to ocean shipping? Why was not the old canal system merely enlarged to 22 feet draft, which would enable lake freighters to go down to Montreal, transship grain, pick up iron ore and take it to the head of the lakes? This could have been done for a fraction of the cost, and it would have served the same purpose. We would then have had a toll-free seaway, an all-Canadian seaway, and all the ships would still go by Cornwall as they have done for the last 100 years. Perhaps part of the answer is that the former minister was ill advised by some of his assistants such as Mr. R. A. C. Henry, who was connected with a company con-

tracting with the Department of Transport while the same Mr. Henry was advising the department. I believe that the former minister of transport deserves full credit for his role on the seaway construction and I believe further that the present Minister of Transport deserves full sympathy for his unenviable task of trying to make the seaway work.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to direct a question to the minister whose estimates are now before us. Is it the minister's intention to comment on the well read speech and charges made by the member for Stormont?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have no intention either of commenting on the speech which the hon. member for Stormont has made, but I am rising to deal with a matter as briefly as I can which was brought up earlier which comes under this head, and that is the construction of the south channel bridge at Cornwall. I do so with a great deal of detachment because the bridge was constructed after I had left the administration of the seaway, although I must admit that the contract was awarded shortly before I left. I desire to deal with it because of some of the statements which were made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, and I believe there are one or two things which have not been brought to the attention of the committee which I would like to deal with at the moment.
The first matter is that it is an international bridge; one-third of it is in Canada and two-thirds is in the United States. By an agreement with the St. Lawrence Seaway Corporation, that is the United States entity, it was agreed that Canada would build the substructure of that bridge and the United States would build the superstructure. It was also agreed that the engineers of the bridge would be Mr. D. B. Steinman, consulting engineer of New York city, who worked in association with Dr. Pratley, now deceased; but the plans and specifications were prepared by Mr. Steinman. The point I am trying to re-emphasize now is that the bridge is one which is located one-third in Canada and two-thirds in the United States.
The other point I am making is that the contract for the substructure was given to a Canadian corporation. Now the Foundation of Canada Engineering Corporation Limited was retained by the St. Lawrence seaway authority to ascertain what effects there were in the piers. It was reported one of the piers on the north side close to Cornwall island had shifted to some extent because it was

Supp ly-Transport
not lying on glacial till although later this proved unfounded. It was, however, a short distance from glacial till; there was some sediment between the bottom of the concrete and the glacial till. After that had been discovered, remedial measures were effected and further examination was made. An independent board of consultants was appointed in order to investigate the measures, and the board of engineers was composed of two United States engineers and a member of the Foundation Company of Canada. And after they had examined the pier they found that the piers were adequate to safely sustain all dead and maximum live loads and that the remedial works which they had recommended had been completed.
The point I want to make is that this was first and foremost a joint Canadian-United States obligation in so far as the construction of the bridge was concerned. It was a purely United States operation in so far as the plans and specifications were concerned. It was a purely Canadian operation in so far as the substructure went, but I am sure that the United States development corporation would never have thought of placing on the substructure the weight of the superstructure unless they had been convinced, as the board of consultants so found, that the weight of the superstructure would be borne by the substructure.
Then there is also the point that this bridge operates between two countries. This bridge, in so far as the piers are concerned, is not unlike some installations of the seaway authority where the walls were placed on glacial till, and from what information I gained I am confident in my mind that there is absolutely nothing the matter with the bridge. I am sorry that the hon. member for Assiniboia, basing his contention on an anonymous informant, made the statement which he did. The statements which he made are serious and far-reaching because they are to the effect that the bridge is doomed. There is not the slightest evidence that the bridge is doomed. On the contrary, there is every evidence that the bridge is in excellent condition, and it seems to me in fairness to those with whom I was associated over a number of years-though I had nothing to do with the execution of the contract- that I should at the first opportunity make the statement that there is nothing wrong regarding the construction of this bridge.
Will you give me time to speak before ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, I will be through in just a moment. Then there is also the point that it is unfortunate that information

such as this should be used in the committee when it is of an anonymous nature. If an hon. member feels that something has gone wrong with construction work and will name the engineer or name the person making the charge, or indicate that the person has a reputation with which he backs the charge, then I think those are conditions which should receive attention, but when a charge is made without foundation and without information of that character, and without sufficient grounds, based on information supplied by an anonymous person, then, I believe, no credence whatever should be given to it.

In view of the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Laurier, I should like to ask whether he and the minister have seen the Toronto Telegram of June 12. I would call their attention to the front page, where it says: "Would go 40 Miles to Shun Bridge". The article, written by a staff reporter, says, and I quote:
The former chief of the St. Lawrence seaway's inspection division says he would drive 40 miles to avoid going over the new Cornwall bridge and that he would not take his family across it under any circumstances.
J. B. Stirling of Montreal offered to come to Ottawa and testify fully if a parliamentary inquiry or a judicial investigation is ordered by the government to study charges that the bridge is unsafe.
May I also draw the attention of the minister and the hon. member for Laurier to what appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of June 11, where it was reported:
M. A. Hanson, divisional engineer on the St. Lawrence seaway, this morning said there was no foundation for reports that the south span of the Cornwall-Massena bridge was improperly constructed.
Since this latter statement is at variance with the information which was given in answer to the question I asked concerning the movement of the piers, and in the light of these reports which appear in the Citizen and in the Telegram, particularly the statement by the former chief of the seaway inspection division, I should like to ask the minister with regard to the statement he made, in all sincerity and honesty, that if he is prepared to have a meeting between the St. Lawrence authority and their engineers-everyone responsible-and those of us who have been asking questions on this matter here in Ottawa; that if his offer is not an offer of a secret or star chamber meeting but will be an open meeting, then we accept it. The hon. member for Laurier has seen what is in the papers, and the affidavits, according to our best information and our personal inspection, and I repeat that if the minister's offer means an open

meeting we accept. I accept right now, and am authorized to do so on behalf of the hon. member for Assiniboia. But I do not accept it if the meeting is to be held as a star chamber meeting.

This talk of a star chamber is the kind of nonsense we have been accustomed to expect from that corner of the house, the kind of nonsense which was talked during the last provincial election, and the result showed what the people in the big province thought of that kind of talk.
1 have offered to have the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Vancouver East meet with any of our officials, and if they are interested in getting all the information they may ask questions freely and take all the time required to digest the information. If they are interested in getting information, that is the way to get it. Nothing will be withheld, and they will be given all the information they desire. If they are interested only in cheap publicity, which appears to be the case, then of course they will not be satisfied with that kind of meeting because at such a meeting the press will not be present; they will not be there really to get information to satisfy their curiosity as to whether this bridge was properly built. I would like to read a report which I have dealing with the bridge, which was given to me by the St. Lawrence seaway authority. It reads as follows:
The design engineering of this bridge, both substructure and superstructure, was the work of
D.	B. Steinman, consulting engineer, New York, under contract with the corps of engineers, United States army, acting in its capacity as contracting agent for the St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation, and P. L. Pratley, deceased, consulting engineer of Montreal, retained by the St. Lawrence seaway authority as Canadian associate consultant, both as agreed to by the two seaway entities.
The piers were designed for and are founded on extreme dense glacial till. The original test borings made at the sites of the main piers disclose dense glacial till overlying bed rock. Borings were taken into the rock. Standard penetration tests disclose material as being extremely dense with a weight of 145 pounds per cubic foot, as compared with 148 pounds for concrete. The glacial till required drilling and blasting to excavate. There has been no settlement from the time the piers were completed and prior to the erection of steel. The factor of safety is at least one and a half under the most extreme conditions of load.
After the piers were erected test borings made in the normal course by seaway engineers revealed a lack of proper bonding between the base of the piers and the glacial till. This was remedied under expert supervision and an engineering board representing both Canadian and United States interests has certified that the piers and the soil on which they rest are now adequate to sufficiently sustain all dead and maximum live loads.

If I may, I should like to say I regret very much that the minister should say that I speak nonsense. He and I are

Answer by: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minisier
of Norihern Affairs and National Resources):
1.	Yes.
2.	Yes.
3.	Dr. MacNeish led various expeditions in order to renew investigations in Mexico at the request of the director of the Harvard University botanical museum and with the approval of the then chief curator of the national museum of Canada. The work was done in the years of 1953, 1954, 1955, 1956 and 1959. During the fiscal years of 1952-53, 1955-56 and 1958-59, work was done wholly on Dr. MacNeish's statutory leave time. Seventy-four days outside duty was granted in 1953-54 and 66 days in 1954-55 in addition to Dr. MacNeish's annual statutory leave. Over the years hundreds of local labourers were hired in the state of Tamaulipas. The department has no record of the persons employed as the expeditions were not organized by the national museum of Canada.
4.	The purposes of the expeditions (which had started in 1945-46 and continued 194849) were, in general, to determine the prehistory in the state of Tamaulipas and adjacent parts of the state of Veracruz, Mexico. The specific purposes changed as information accrued. Notably after 1953, the purposes were to determine the origin, spread and the improvements in new world agriculture. The detailed purposes of each expedition, most of the places investigated and the results of expeditions will be found in the following publications by Dr. MacNeish:
(1)	An Early Archaeological Site near Panuco, Veracruz. Transactions of the American Philosophical Society, vol. 44, pt. 4, Philadelphia, Pa., 1954.

(3)	(Co-author with F. Peterson) Santa Marta Rockshelter, Ocozocoautla, Chiapas, Mexico. New World Archaeological Foundation.
(4)	Prehistoric Southeast Mexico Relationships in Light of an Archaeological Survey of Tamaulipas, Mexico. Dissertation for the degree of Ph.D. University of Chicago, library, 1948.
(5)	(Co-author with P. C. Mangelsdorf and W. C. Galinat) Archaeological Evidences on the Diffusion and Evolution of Maize in Northeastern Mexico. Harvard University botanical museum leaflets, vol. 17, No. 5, Cambridge, 1956.
(6)	Prehistoric Settlement Patterns on the Northeastern Periphery of Meso-America in Prehistoric Settlement Patterns in the New World edited by G. R. Willey, Viking Fund Publication in Anthropology, No. 23, New York, 1956.
(7)	(Co-author with T. W. Whitaker and H. C. Cutler) Cucurbit Materials from Three Caves near Ocampo, Tamaulipas. American Antiquity, vol. 22, No. 4, Salt Lake City, Utah, 1957.
(8)	The Independent Investigator in The Identification of Nonartifactual Archaeological Materials. Ed. Walter W. Taylor. National Academy of Sciences-national research council, publication 565, 1957. Washington,

(9)	(Co-author with L. Kaplan) Prehistoric Bean Remains from Caves in the Ocampo Region, Mexico. Submitted for publication to Harvard University botanical museum leaflets.

(10)	A Preliminary Report on Coastal Tamaulipas, Mexico. American Antiquity, vol. 13, No. 1, Menasha, Wise., July 1947.

(12)	The Development of Agriculture and the Concomitant Development of Civilization in Meso-America, Tamaulipas, Mexico. American Philosophical Society year book, 1954, Philadelphia, Pa., 1955.

(17)	Archaeological Discoveries in Northern Mexico. International News Service, New York, 1949.
(18)	Ancient Maize and Mexico. Archaeology, vol. 8, No. 2, Brattleboro, Vt., 1955.

U.S. Naval Forces on Great Lakes

subtopic: EXCHANGE OF NOTES RESPECTING U.S. NAVAL FORCES ON GREAT LAKES No. 178

speechtext:
The ambassador of the United States of America presents his compliments to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and has the honour to refer to the Rush-Bagot treaty of 1817, which serves to guide Canada and the United States in matters relating to naval forces on the great lakes.
The ambassador wishes to state that the United States navy, in conjunction with the St. Lawrence seaway opening ceremonies and the Chicago international fair in July 1959, has proposed that its amphibious squadron eight (PHIBRON 8), with marines embarked conduct demonstration and training assault landings in the great lakes area. This project has been designated Operation Inland Sea. The location for the proposed landing area has not yet been determined.
The ambassador is authorized to extend an invitation for the Royal Canadian Navy to participate in this operation, thereby making it a combined Canadian-United States exercise, and to express the hope that the Canadian government will share the view of the United States government that this exercise would not be inconsistent with the intent of the Rush-Bagot treaty of 1817.
The ambassador would appreciate the consideration of the Canadian government with respect to this proposal.
Embassy of the United States of America, Ottawa, February 13, 1959.

The ambassador of the United States of America presents his compliments to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and has the honour to refer to the ambassador's Note No. 178 of February 13, 1959, concerning a proposal of the United States navy to have its amphibious squadron eight (PHIBRON 8), with marines embarked, conduct demonstration and training assault landings in the great lakes area.
In conjunction with this project, which has been designated Operation Inland Sea, the ambassador wishes to state that the United States navy proposes to send a task force consisting of about 28 ships including the heavy cruiser Macon on a tour of 24 United States ports in the great lakes area this summer. The cruise would begin shortly after June 26 and continue through July 27. Some of the ships would participate in the previously mentioned amphibious demonstration. The task force commander would be Rear Admiral E. B. Taylor commander of
destroyer forces Atlantic fleet. The task force would be composed of two destroyer squadrons one amphibious squadron four submarines, the heavy cruiser Macon and the frigate Mitscher (DL-2).
The ambassador would be most appreciative if the Canadian government would find it possible at an early date to concur in the view of the United States government that this good-will cruise would not be inconsistent with the intent of the Rush-Bagot treaty of 1817. In the event that the Canadian government concurs in this view the United States navy would plan to issue a press release in the near future along the above lines.
Embassy of the United States of America, Ottawa, March 9, 1959.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs presents his compliments to the embassador of the United States of America and has the honour to refer to the ambassador's notes No. 178 of February 13, 1959 and No. 207 of March 9, 1959 relating to the Rush-Bagot agreement of 1817 and containing an invitation for Canadian naval units to participate in certain exercises being planned by the United States navy in the waters of the great lakes.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs notes that it is proposed that 28 ships of the United States navy carry out a good-will cruise of United States lake ports as well as demonstrations and training assault landing exercises in the United States waters of the great lakes.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has the pleasure to inform the ambassador that the government of Canada shares the view of the United States government that the naval movements required for these proposed operations would not be inconsistent with the intent of the Rush-Bagot agreement of 1817 whose application and interpretation are more fully elaborated in notes related thereto exchanged between the Canadian and United States governments on November 18, 1946 and December 5, 1946 respectively.
A further communication can be expected relating to the invitation, extended in the ambassador's note No. 178 of February 13, for Canadian naval units to participate in the proposed exercises.
